thread.title: IRS Allows Churches to Endorse Political Candidates in Religious Services
thread.title_full: IRS Allows Churches to Endorse Political Candidates in Religious Services

author: Rudy Blalock
title: IRS Allows Churches to Endorse Political Candidates in Religious Services
text:
The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has clarified that houses of worship may endorse political candidates during religious services without losing their tax-exempt status, marking a shift in how decades-old restrictions are interpreted.
In a court filing on Monday to resolve a lawsuit by two Texas churches and the National Religious Broadcasters, the IRS said traditional religious communications are exempt from a provision in the U.S. tax code that bars nonprofits—religious and secular—from endorsing political candidates.
President Donald Trump praised the development Wednesday, telling White House reporters he welcomes the change.
"I love the fact that churches could endorse a political candidate," Trump said. "If somebody of faith wants to endorse, I think it's something that I'd like to hear."
arguedthe Johnson Amendment "unconstitutionally prohibits § 501(c)(3) [non-profit, tax-exempt] organizations from engaging in political speech."
Johnson Amendment
The amendment, introduced by former President Lyndon B. Johnson during his tenure in the Senate, was added to the federal tax code when Johnson faced political opponents accusing him of having communist sympathies.The law states that tax-exempt groups "are absolutely prohibited from directly or indirectly participating in, or intervening in, any political campaign on behalf of (or in opposition to) any candidate for elective public office."
IRS clarificationrepresents a narrower exception than what the plaintiffs sought. According to the agency's court submission, the interpretation maintains existing practices rather than creating new policy.
wrotein its court submission.
The filing noted that the IRS "generally has not enforced the Johnson Amendment against houses of worship for speech concerning electoral politics in the context of worship services”.
Trump has long criticized the Johnson Amendment's restrictions on religious political expression. During his first presidential campaign, he promised evangelical leaders he would work to repeal the law.
saidin 2016. "I am going to work very hard to repeal that language and to protect free speech for all Americans."
signedan executive order directing the IRS to ease enforcement of the political activity ban for churches.
"Those people were not allowed to speak up. Now they're allowed to speak up," Trump said Wednesday. "I think it's terrific."
The Justice Department, under President Joe Biden, had previously defended the law's constitutionality, arguing that Congress was entitled to refuse to subsidize political activity through tax benefits.
The IRS stated the exception applies to "communications from a house of worship” in the same filing.
